prudent

PROO-dent -- shares a root with 'provident,' meaning to plan ahead wisely. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prudent is showing care and good judgment, especially about practical matters.

Waiting until the storm passed before driving home was the prudent decision.

Example

Before signing the lease, a prudent young renter carefully reads every clause, asks the landlord several questions, and calculates whether the rent truly fits her monthly budget.

That careful, sensible weighing of a decision before acting is what makes her prudent. Unlike 'lucky,' which is about chance, prudent describes deliberate good judgment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cautious: Cautious means careful to avoid danger or mistakes, and it can shade into holding back. Prudent is about sound judgment rather than avoidance: a prudent person weighs the practical risks and still acts when the choice makes sense.

farsighted: Farsighted means thinking well ahead and planning for what may come years from now. Prudent judgment can be immediate -- a sensible call made on the spot -- while farsighted always points to the distant future.

level-headed: Level-headed describes staying calm and clear-thinking under pressure -- not panicking when things go wrong. Prudent is about the quality of the judgment itself: a prudent choice weighs practical risks well, whether or not anyone is under pressure.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reckless: without thought for the consequences of an action

rash: acting without careful thought

Where it sits · how carefully the choice is weighed — sensible → prudent → judicious

sensible vs. prudent: Sensible is a more everyday word than prudent -- sensible just means showing good sense in daily choices, while prudent carries a more formal, deliberate weighing of risk.

judicious vs. prudent: Judicious can feel even more careful than prudent: prudent suggests general good sense, while judicious specifically implies a careful, almost judge-like weighing of a decision.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — prud-

root — prud-: foresight, practical wisdom (Latin (prudentia, from providentia))

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: doing or being; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin prudentia meant 'foresight, practical wisdom' -- shortened from providentia, 'seeing ahead' -- and the suffix -ent forms the adjective. A prudent person is one who sees ahead and plans wisely.

Use the root in a new word: provident

Use the root in a new word: provident: Their provident planning meant the family had savings set aside for years of college tuition.
